about: The Edge Lab's lessons and real examples, in one place. The research page (web/src/pages/EdgeLab.tsx) and the public page /learn/edge-lab/ (scripts/seo/build_public.py) both read this file, so they never disagree. Links: doc = a doc id, ref = a key in references.json, term = a glossary id, page = a research page hash (dropped on the public page).
intro: An edge is a reason to expect a trading rule to keep making money after costs. Most edges found in a backtest are not real. They come from luck, from using data before it was public, or from prices nobody could trade at. These lessons are the checks we use on our own ideas, each with a real mistake we made and caught.

lessons.title: Write the idea down before you test it
lessons.text: Say what the signal is, what it trades, how you will judge it and what counts as failure, before you see any result. Once you have seen a chart, every later choice bends toward it, even when you do not mean it to.
lessons.do: Every official run is registered first: the plan is written down and the exact code is locked before the run. Only runs in the sealed record count as results.

links.label: Official results come only from the ledger

lessons.title: Keep some data you have never looked at
lessons.text: A rule built on the past will always look good on that past. Build on one stretch of history, then test once on a stretch you never touched. If you peek at the holdout and change the rule, it is no longer a holdout. The best holdout is time: data that did not exist when you wrote the rule down.
lessons.do: Our tests check every era and the last five years on their own. We also say plainly that none of this is truly out of sample: only data that arrives after 2026-10-20 is genuinely new, which is why registered strategies keep being tracked.

lessons.title: Count every trade's cost, then ask how much cost it can survive
lessons.text: A rule that trades every day pays the spread and fees every day, and small costs add up to more than most edges earn. Work out the breakeven cost: the cost per trade at which the gain falls to zero. If it is close to what you would really pay, there is no edge.
lessons.do: Every backtest charges trading costs, and one of the eleven tests doubles them. Paper factor portfolios pay an estimated yearly cost: 0.5% to 1% for slow factors, 3% for momentum and 10% for short-term reversal.

lessons.title: Every variation you try is a trial
lessons.text: Try enough rules and one will look great by luck alone. Changing a window from 20 days to 25 is another trial, and so is a new asset or a new start date. The deflated Sharpe ratio raises the bar for how many tries you made and how widely their results spread.
lessons.do: Our always-on search tries about 20,000 variations an hour. It keeps every attempt, failed ones included, and recomputes the luck check with the total count. Its finds are leads, not results.

lessons.title: Use data only from the moment it was public
lessons.text: A backtest may only use what a trader could have known at the time. A monthly average is known only after the month ends. The CFTC's Commitments of Traders report shows positions as of Tuesday but is released on Friday. US jobless claims for a week come out the following Thursday. Company results arrive weeks after the quarter ends and are often revised. Prices that share a date can still close hours apart.
lessons.do: Monthly averages are used only from a week after month end. A test cuts the data at several dates and fails any strategy whose earlier positions change, and the search applies the same check to its random variations.

links.label: A look-ahead test for every strategy

lessons.title: Ask how much money fits, and who else knows
lessons.text: An edge in a small, thinly traded market can vanish once you trade real size, because your own orders move the price. Published edges also attract money. McLean and Pontiff (2016) found that stock return patterns earned about 58% less after the paper describing them came out.
lessons.do: Every idea in the algorithm library records where it came from and when it was first published, with what happened after publication where it is known. One of our tests looks at the last five years alone, because published ideas tend to fade.

lessons.title: Distrust results that look too good
lessons.text: A huge Sharpe ratio is more often a bug than a discovery. A rule that sits in cash most of the time barely moves, so its Sharpe ratio can look enormous on a handful of trades. Prices nobody could trade at, such as a monthly average, an index level or spot natural gas, can show gains nobody could have earned.
lessons.do: The search rejects any variation that sits in cash 95% or more of the time. A percent change through a zero or negative price earns nothing. Spot gas is used only as a signal until we have futures data.

examples.title: Stocks while copper rises
examples.text: It looked like the best rule we had found. Copper came as a monthly average, which is known only after the month ends, but the backtest used it from the first day. Once we added a one-week delay after month end, the gain disappeared. Copper is now never held, because nobody can trade at a monthly average.

examples.title: Natural gas into winter
examples.text: It led the strategy race at +2,632%. The gain came from holding spot natural gas through price spikes, including an 85% jump in one day in January 2024. Spot gas is not something anyone trades. We removed the strategy on 22 October 2026, and gas is a signal only until we have futures data.

examples.title: Brent against WTI, a few hours early
examples.text: Brent closes in London hours before WTI closes in New York, so two prices with the same date were not set at the same moment. Acting on both the same day turned a Sharpe ratio of 0.5 into 1.2. The pair trade now acts a day late.

examples.title: Variations that hide in cash
examples.text: A variation that is in cash nearly all the time hardly moves. Dividing its small return by its tiny risk gives a huge Sharpe ratio that means nothing. Among thousands of random variations, these float to the top. The search rejects any variation in cash 95% or more of the time.

examples.title: Oil below zero
examples.text: US oil (WTI) closed at minus $37 on 20 April 2020. A percent change through a negative price produced a 110% loss in a single day, which no position could have had. A percent change through zero or below now earns nothing.
